name: Sam Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead three farm-policy clerks at an insurer because I am good at catching a wrong equipment number. I use AI occasionally to summarise long endorsements, but read the signed exclusions myself. Nia, my partner, works at a bakery counter; we have no children, and lower lead pay plus a car repair leave us renting with just over two weeks of expenses saved and few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the farm-policy desk that a little AI help can find a clause faster, but a damaged tractor still has to match the machine named on the policy. I use AI occasionally to summarise long endorsements, then check the serial number and exclusions myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead three clerks because I am good at catching a wrong machine number. This small insurer pays below the usual lead rate; my partner Nia works at a bakery counter, and after a car repair we rent with just over two weeks of expenses saved and no children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking farm-equipment claim forms against policy serial numbers each Wednesday. We would cancel one streaming subscription and save 20 monthly only while both wages cover rent and car-running costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious even if AI stays small. A tyre and a rent payment landed in the same week last month, and the buffer barely survived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What serial number error did you find?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A claimant photographed one tractor but the policy listed the older machine. I asked for the purchase record before the claim was priced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI sometimes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It points me to a long endorsement quickly. I still read the exclusion and the machine number before I send a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking writing, checking, buying and customer answers could process routine tractor endorsements before a clerk sees them. A person should still explain why a costly part is excluded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if one reviewer handles the AI output for several policy desks. Two weeks saved and few nearby insurers make a cut frightening, even though I am open to a tool that proves itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for approved paid time to learn a new AI endorsement checker on invented tractor policies. If approved, I’d test one wrong serial each week with a senior underwriter reviewing the result; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local policy-support vacancies only if wages cover rent, car costs and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, but I would rather test the checker than argue about a demo. A polished exclusion letter can still name the wrong tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an invented policy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put one model number on the application and another on the claim, with no real customer data. The underwriter would say whether the tool found the mismatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid time is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current checks and ask for written hours notice. I would not run the new tool on customer files by myself.

S1.quote: A polished exclusion letter can still name the wrong tractor.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** goes beyond occasional summaries and needs paid approval on invented policies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could read farm policies, price claims and answer customers cheaper than our desk. Robots inspecting tractors and doing bakery counter work may follow around 2031, after the paperwork changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead clerk role could end quickly, and two weeks saved would not carry rent through a search. Nia’s bakery wage helps, but it cannot cover the car and all our bills alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d cancel the subscription now and ask for written notice of policy-desk cuts. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local farm-parts counter openings only if they exist and wages cover rent, car costs and basic bills; I would ask the public employment office what support we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my wage. A policy on a tractor will not put fuel in my car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know farm parts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped my uncle label parts in his shop as a teenager, but that does not mean a shop owes me a job. I would ask which paid vacancies actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to a larger insurance market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would look at local insurers and parts shops first. Nia’s bakery job and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach policy paperwork first.
I expect **tractor robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead clerk wage** could end.
I know **two weeks saved** cannot carry rent for long.
do: **Cancel subscription** and request written desk-cut notice now.
**Apply for paid parts-counter** after 2028 loss only if local vacancies cover rent, car costs and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
feel: **Alarmed** about a lost wage and rent.
S2.quote: A policy on a tractor will not put fuel in my car.
fieldNote: His **old shop exposure** is small and does not guarantee paid parts work.
He asks about **actual public eligibility** without assuming a benefit replaces his wage.

steps.text: Cancel streaming subscription when policy-desk cuts threaten

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to see which farm-equipment customers still need a person at the counter. Robots inspecting tractors and serving bakery customers may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could test whether I still like parts work while I earn the insurance wage, but I cannot afford an unpaid Saturday. I remember boxes from my uncle’s shop, not the current stock system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a local equipment shop for one paid Saturday stock shift a month and ask my insurer to approve outside work. If a paid vacancy exists, covers travel and both agree, I’d learn the current parts register from the shift lead; we would save 30 monthly only while both wages cover rent and car costs, and after 2031 claim-job loss I’d apply for paid local parts roles only if wages cover rent, car costs and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the policy desk but steadier after a real shift. An unpaid Saturday would use the last of my fuel money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn at the counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would match a part number to the machine model and ask the lead to check my stock entry. I would not sell a safety-critical part alone on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no Saturday place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the insurance job while it pays and ask again later. I would not call a chat with the shop manager training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives a young clerk time to build a reserve and see whether parts work pays. Robots inspecting machines and serving counters may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have many working years ahead, but I cannot make the present two-week buffer last by thinking about 2036. If both wages hold, we might save several months of rent; the policy desk could still shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking policy serials and save 45 monthly only while both wages cover rent and car costs. I’d take a paid parts shift quarterly only if a vacancy exists, travel is covered and my insurer approves outside work; if my clerk job ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid local parts openings only if wages cover rent, car costs and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d remain anxious about current money even with a decade. A plan for a future parts job does not pay this month’s car insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you quit insurance for the parts shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep the main wage while it lasts. One quarterly shift is evidence about the work, not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Nia’s family help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would not put anyone else’s wages in our budget. Nia and I need to decide from jobs and bills we actually have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead claim wage could disappear before a paid local parts opening exists. Written notice, a real vacancy covering rent and car costs, and verified temporary public help would matter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a paid Saturday means I can live on farm parts. One Saturday is a test of work, not a second salary.

headlineQuote: One Saturday is a test of work, not a second salary.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old policy lead** with a bachelor’s degree, lower pay and just over two weeks saved.
He and Nia **rent together**, with no children and car costs still to cover.
He **uses AI occasionally** for summaries but checks signed exclusions himself.
He tests **paid parts shifts** only with shop vacancies, covered travel and insurer approval.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his insurance wage before paid local parts work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a rent-and-car-covering vacancy and verified public help would matter.
